newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebel leader takes salute from turncoat troops.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel leader takes salute from turncoat troops.

text.p: Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Saturday took the salute from 400 "re-educated" ex-government soldiers who defected to his ranks.
"It was a good day. We have witnessed the soldiers of the FAZ (Zaire army) who have been re-educated," Kabila said after watching the soldiers goose-step past him at Goma's airport.
The soldiers, many of whom defected after being captured when Goma fell last November, were passing out after a four- month retraining programme.

Dressed in green camouflage and watched by hundreds of rebel troops sitting on the grass around the strip the soldiers shouted:"We swear allegiance to president Laurent Kabila and we swear allegiance to the Alliance."
The rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) have taken control of more than a third of the country since launching their campaign last October.
Mining sources in Zaire's diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi said the rebels entered the town early on Saturday.
Speaking to Reuters from the centre of the town, they said rebels had streamed in across a bridge during the morning.
Asked about this Kabila told reporters with a twinkle in his eye and a glance at his watch: "Naturally it (Mbuji-Mayi) is yet to fall."
The Alliance is now closing in on the second city Lubumbashi, capital of Shaba region, its advance slowed more by Zaire's huge distances than by resistance from the government army.

Senior rebel military commanders argue government troops loot and flee rather than fight because they lack legitimacy and realise time has run out for Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko who has ruled since 1965 but is now ailing with cancer.
Saturday's parade caused chaos at the airport as jets swooped low over a runway turned into a public highway by bystanders who had come to watch.
Two planes approached the runway at house-height only to pull up when they saw it was packed with children, both planes landed at the second or third attempt.
Territorial gains have enabled rebels who were virtually unheard of six months ago to maintain an inflexible bargaining position demanding that Mobutu must resign.
Success has also radically altered the role of Kabila, since 1967 the leader of an obscure guerrilla force of ethnic Banyamulenge in South Kivu region.
"He is no longer the figurehead of an ethnic group fighting for survival. Now he represents the revenge of the people against Mobutu," one senior aid official told Reuters.
